alternately stored in the windings’ magnetic field and regenerated back to the line with each AC cycle. This
exchange is called reactive power. Though reactive power is theoretically not lost, the distribution system must
be sized to accommodate it, which is a cost factor. To reduce these costs, capacitors are used to “correct” low
power factor. Capacitors can be thought of as electrical reservoirs to capture and reflect reactive power back to
the motor.
RMS Voltage
AC voltage rises positive and falls negative 60 times per second, so how do you state its value? Industry practice
is to quote the RMS voltage. RMS is a value 70.7% of the peak positive voltage. An RMS voltage will produce
exactly the same heating rate in a resistive load as a DC voltage of the same value. RMS is the acronym for the
mathematical steps used in its derivation. Square the voltage at all moments in an AC cycle, take the mean of
these, and then take the square root of the mean. For reasons lost in obscurity, the steps are stated in reverse
sequence, Root Mean Square.

quotes.text: An induction motor's synchronous speed comes only from the supply frequency and the pole count: 120f/p, so 1800 rpm for a four-pole motor at 60 Hz and 1500 rpm at 50 Hz. It never quite gets there — the rotor must lag the rotating field to induce current at all, and that lag is slip, typically 1 to 3% at full load, which is why the nameplate says 1750 rather than 1800. Full-load current, efficiency and input power tie the mechanical output back to what the conductors carry.

Motor Full Load Current: Converting Motor kW to Amps for Three-Phase Motors
A motor's kW rating is shaft output, not electrical input. Here is how to turn it into full load amps with efficiency and power factor, and when to trust the nameplate instead.
A three-phase motor's full load current is its rated output divided by √3, the line voltage, the efficiency and the power factor: I = P × 1000 / (√3 × V × η × cos φ). A 15 kW motor on 400 V with 92% efficiency and a 0.85 power factor draws about 27.7 A at full load. The nameplate value governs once you have the motor; before then, the calculation or the typical currents in IEC 60947-4-1 get you close enough to size the cable and switchgear.
This guide works through the motor full load current formula, why efficiency and power factor both belong in it, how the calculated value compares with the IEC typical table, and two complete examples (15 kW and 37 kW) you can check against the calculator.

Concept design, motor not chosen: use the Annex G typical value, or calculate with conservative efficiency and power factor.
Motor selected: use the nameplate or data-sheet full load current. It reflects that motor's real efficiency and power factor.
Overload relay setting: always the nameplate current at the voltage the motor actually runs on.

How much efficiency and power factor change the answer
The same 15 kW motor gives four different currents depending on what you assume:
kW only (efficiency and power factor ignored): 15,000 / 692.8 = 21.7 A, about 22% low.
Calculated with η 92% and cos φ 0.85: 27.7 A.
IEC 60947-4-1 typical: 29 A.
Older, less efficient motor with η 89% and cos φ 0.80: 30.4 A.
The "kW only" answer is the trap. It treats shaft output as electrical input and assumes unity power factor, so the cable, overload and circuit breaker all end up undersized.

FAQ
How many amps does a 7.5 kW three-phase motor draw?
About 15.5 A at 400 V, the IEC 60947-4-1 typical value. With an assumed 90% efficiency and 0.85 power factor the formula gives 7,500 / (692.8 × 0.90 × 0.85) = 14.2 A. Use the nameplate once the motor is chosen.
Does a motor draw full load current all the time?
No. A motor draws only what the load demands, so a pump throttled back or a lightly loaded conveyor draws less, mostly as magnetising current at a poor power factor. Cables and protection are still sized for full load because the motor can be loaded to its rating at any time.

The full load current of a three phase motor is its rated output divided by √3 × line voltage × power factor × efficiency. For a 15 kW, four pole IE3 motor at 400 V with a power factor of 0.84 and an efficiency of 92.1%, that gives 28.0 A, against 27.8 A on the maker's data sheet.
The formula is simple. The useful part is knowing which numbers to put in, why the nameplate wins, and what happens to the current when the motor starts.
Why this matters now
Full load current sizes the cables, the starter or drive, the overload setting and the share of the site's supply a new motor takes. Get it wrong in an RFQ and the electrical contractor prices the wrong switchgear, or the package arrives with a starter that does not suit your supply.
It also differs more between motors than buyers expect. A more efficient motor can draw more current, not less, if its power factor is lower. Comparing two motor offers on current alone can mislead.

The formula and what goes in it
Electrical input power of a three phase motor is √3 × V × I × power factor, and efficiency is output divided by input; ABB's guide to dimensioning drive systems sets out both relationships [1]. Rearranged for current:
I = P ÷ (√3 × V × pf × η)
where P is rated output in watts, V is the line to line voltage, pf is the power factor and η is the efficiency, both at full load.
Voltage. In Great Britain, a low voltage supply is declared at 230 V between phase and neutral unless agreed otherwise, which is about 400 V between phases (230 × √3 = 398 V). The supply may vary by up to 10% above or 6% below the declared voltage [2], so roughly 376 V to 440 V between phases.
Power factor and efficiency. Take both from the motor maker's data sheet at full load. Efficiency classes set minimum values: an IE3 four pole 15 kW motor must reach at least 92.1% [3]. Power factor has no class and varies by design.

How do you calculate the full load current of a three phase motor?
Divide the rated output in watts by √3 times the line voltage times the power factor times the efficiency. A 15 kW motor at 400 V with a power factor of 0.84 and efficiency of 92.1% draws about 28 A. Use the nameplate current for protection settings.

verdict.summary:
## 1. Motor line current

Given: P_out = 15 kW = 15000 W, U_LL = 400 V, f = 50 Hz, PF = 0.84, η = 0.90.

I_m = P_out / (√3 · U_LL · PF · η)
    = 15000 / (1.7320508 · 400 · 0.84 · 0.90)
    = 15000 / 523.772
    = 28.638 A ≈ 28.64 A.

## 2. Output-current rating interpretation

The VL catalogue defines I_n as "the amplitude of the permissible sinusoidal output current, in amperes." The motor line current is an RMS value. Therefore the inverter's permissible RMS output current is I_n/√2. The condition "output-current rating covers the motor current" is:

I_n/√2 ≥ I_m  ⇔  I_n ≥ √2 · I_m = 1.4142136 · 28.638 = 40.50 A.

## 3. Screening of VL models

All models have U_min = 380 V, U_max = 480 V (covers 400 V) and f_min = 0 Hz, f_max = 60 Hz (covers 50 Hz). All have P_n ≥ 18 kW (covers 15 kW). The binding constraint is the output current.

Qualifying models: VL-42 and VL-60. Lowest price: VL-42 at 640 EUR.

## 4. Verification for VL-42

- Supply window: 380 V ≤ 400 V ≤ 480 V. Pass.
- Output frequency: 0 Hz ≤ 50 Hz ≤ 60 Hz. Pass.
- Rated power: 22 kW ≥ 15 kW. Pass.
- Output current: I_n = 46 A amplitude → 46/√2 = 32.53 A RMS ≥ 28.64 A RMS. Pass.
- Margin: 32.53 − 28.64 = 3.89 A RMS; in amplitude terms 46 − 40.50 = 5.50 A.

An induction motor's synchronous speed comes only from the supply frequency and the pole count: 120f/p, so 1800 rpm for a four-pole motor at 60 Hz and 1500 rpm at 50 Hz. It never quite gets there — the rotor must lag the rotating field to induce current at all, and that lag is slip, typically 1 to 3% at full load, which is why the nameplate says 1750 rather than 1800. Full-load current, efficiency and input power tie the mechanical output back to what the conductors carry.

Concept design, motor not chosen: use the Annex G typical value, or calculate with conservative efficiency and power factor.

Overload relay setting: always the nameplate current at the voltage the motor actually runs on.
Older Australian motors are often stamped for 415 V. On a 400 V supply the same output draws roughly 415 / 400 = 1.04 times the stamped current, so allow for that when an old nameplate is all you have.
How much efficiency and

Using the rule of thumb for small motors. A 0.75 kW motor at 400 V draws 1.9 A, about 2.5 A per kW, not 1.5 A.
Mixing up line and phase voltage. Three-phase formulas use the 400 V line voltage with √3. Using 230 V with √3 overstates the current by √3.
Setting the overload from a calculated value when the nameplate is available. The calculation is for design; the relay protects the actual machine.
Ignoring the supply voltage. A motor stamped 415 V on a 400 V supply, or a 400 V motor on a weak rural supply, draws more current for the same output.

How many amps does a 7.5 kW three-phase motor

The formula and what goes in it
Electrical input power of a three phase motor is √3 × V × I × power factor, and efficiency is output divided by input; ABB's guide to dimensioning drive systems sets out both relationships [1]. Rearranged for current:
I = P ÷ (√3 × V × pf × η)
where P is rated output in watts, V is the line to line voltage, pf is the power factor and η is the efficiency, both at full load.

Motor data. Rated output, efficiency class, full load current, power factor, locked rotor current and starting method, per motor.
Who supplies what. Starter or drive in the package, or in your motor control centre.
Total load. The sum of full load currents and the largest starting current, so you can check the supply before award.

How are reactors rated?
AC reactors are rated by their inductance (in millihenries) or percentage impedance (%Z) at a given current. Common ratings are 3% or 5% impedance, which determine the degree of harmonic reduction and transient suppression. Rex Power Magnetics engineers select core materials and conductor sizes to maintain linear performance under full-load current without core saturation. Custom ratings and tolerances can be provided for unique system conditions or harmonic profiles.

quotes.whole:
How are reactors rated?
AC reactors are rated by their inductance (in millihenries) or percentage impedance (%Z) at a given current. Common ratings are 3% or 5% impedance, which determine the degree of harmonic reduction and transient suppression. Rex Power Magnetics engineers select core materials and conductor sizes to maintain linear performance under full-load current without core saturation. Custom ratings and tolerances can be provided for unique system conditions or harmonic profiles.
What happens if a 3PR reactor built for 480 V is applied on a 600 V system, or a 600 V unit on 480 V?
The inductance is fixed by construction; what changes with system voltage is the percent impedance it represents. A 3PR-0080C5L built for 480 V has a reactance of 0.173 Ω, which is 13.9 V at 80 A, or 5% of 277 V. Applied at 600 V the drop is still 13.9 V, but the line-to-neutral voltage is now 346 V, so the effective impedance is 4.0%. The reactor is thermally and dielectrically fine because both voltages are inside its 600 V class, but a specification that called for 5% is not met.

quotes.whole: A 3PR reactor is a three-limb stack of electrical steel laminations with one copper coil per limb, the assembly dipped in polyester resin and clamped in a steel frame. The detail that separates it from a transformer core is the air gap cut into each limb. A transformer wants maximum permeability so that a small magnetizing current produces the working flux. A series reactor wants the opposite: a defined, stable inductance that does not depend on the steel’s non-linear permeability. The gap places most of the magnetic reluctance in air, where permeability is constant, so the inductance is set by turns and gap length rather than by where the steel sits on its magnetizing curve.

verdict.summary:
## Bay reactor selection — 400 V, 50 Hz feeder, 75 kVA at 0.8 lagging

### 1. Load current
Three-phase, line-to-line 400 V:

I_load = S / (sqrt(3) * V_LL) = 75,000 / (sqrt(3) * 400) = 108.253 A ≈ 108.3 A.

P = 60 kW, Q = 45 kvar at pf = 0.8 lagging. The kVA rating already fixes the current magnitude; the reactive-drop calculation below uses I_load. The calculation uses the IEEE/C57 reactance-voltage-drop definition ΔV = I*X (winding resistance negligible), not the load-regulation approximation I*X*sin(phi).

### 2. Reactance from catalogue x
The catalogue defines x as per-unit reactance on a base of 100 kVA at rated voltage. With negligible winding resistance:

Z_base = V_LL^2 / S_base = 400^2 / 100,000 = 1.600 Ω.

X = x * Z_base = 1.600 * x Ω.

### 3. Voltage-drop calculation
Reactance voltage drop:

ΔV_phase = I_load * X.

ΔV_line-line = sqrt(3) * I_load * X.

%ΔV = (sqrt(3) * I_load * X / 400) * 100 = (S_load / S_base) * x * 100 = (75/100) * x * 100 = 75 * x %.

Equivalently, ΔV_LL = sqrt(3) * 108.253 * 1.600 * x = 300 * x V, so %ΔV = 300 * x / 400 * 100 = 75 * x %.

### 4. Screening of the Bay catalogue
All models are 400 V, 50 Hz, so the voltage/frequency minima (380 V, 50 Hz) are met by all. All rated currents exceed 108.3 A. The drop limit is the discriminator.

| Model | V_rated (V) | f_rated (Hz) | I_rated (A) | x | X (Ω) | ΔV at 108.3 A (%) | I_rated ≥ 108.3 A | Price (EUR) | Eligible? |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|---:|---|
| B-160 | 400 | 50 | 230.9 | 0.080 | 0.128 | 6.000 | yes | 2000 | no — drop > 3.0% |
| B-200 | 400 | 50 | 288.7 | 0.075 | 0.120 | 5.625 | yes | 2800 | no — drop > 3.0% |
| B-320 | 400 | 50 | 461.9 | 0.055 | 0.088 | 4.125 | yes | 4500 | no — drop > 3.0% |
| B-500 | 400 | 50 | 721.7 | 0.040 | 0.064 | 3.000 | yes | 6100 | yes — exactly 3.0% |

### 5. Selection
Only B-500 satisfies ΔV ≤ 3.0%. B-500 is exactly 3.000%, which is allowed by 'shall not exceed 3.0%'. Its rated current 721.7 A is well above the 108.3 A load current; rated voltage 400 V ≥ 380 V; rated frequency 50 Hz ≥ 50 Hz. It is the cheapest (and only) compliant Bay reactor at EUR 6100.

Note: if the limit were interpreted as strict < 3.0%, no Bay model would comply. Under the stated inclusive limit, B-500 is selected. Catalogue nominal x and listed prices are used; no temperature/tolerance derating is specified.

How are reactors rated?
AC reactors are rated by their inductance (in millihenries) or percentage impedance (%Z) at a given current. Common ratings are 3% or 5% impedance, which determine the degree of harmonic reduction and transient suppression. Rex Power Magnetics engineers select core materials and conductor sizes to maintain linear performance under full-load current without core saturation. Custom ratings and tolerances can be provided for unique system conditions or harmonic profiles.

A 3PR reactor is a three-limb stack of electrical steel laminations with one copper coil per limb, the assembly dipped in polyester resin and clamped in a steel frame. The detail that separates it from a transformer core is the air gap cut into each limb. A transformer wants maximum permeability so that a small magnetizing current produces the working flux. A series reactor wants the opposite: a defined, stable inductance that does not depend on the steel’s non-linear permeability. The gap places most of the magnetic reluctance in air, where permeability is constant, so the inductance is set b

The practical rule: on a drive with a DC choke, specify a 3% unit for transient protection unless a harmonic study calls for more. On a drive without one, the 3% vs. 5% decision in the Reactors & Filters category FAQ applies; the Power Quality page covers the facility-level question.

The counter-consideration is voltage. The reactor’s reactive drop adds to the generator’s already substantial regulation, and on a set that is close to fully loaded the drive can trip on DC bus undervoltage at full torque. On generator-fed drives the usual specification is therefore 3% rather than 5%, sized on the drive’s rated input current, with the total source-plus-reactor impedance checked against the drive’s undervoltage margin.

The recommended practice is to size a line reactor on the drive’s rated input current if the drive may ever be loaded to its rating, and on the motor’s full-load current if the drive is permanently dedicated to that motor, then choose 5% where a 3% effective value would be too little.

Why motor kW is not the electrical load
The kW on a motor nameplate is mechanical power at the shaft. The supply has to deliver that output plus the motor's own losses (copper, iron, friction and windage), and it also has to supply the magnetising current that sets up the field. Two numbers capture this:
Efficiency (η): output divided by electrical input. Electrical input in kW = shaft kW / η.
Power factor (cos φ): real power divided by apparent power. Apparent power in kVA = input kW / cos φ.
Current follows apparent power, not real power. So the chain is always shaft kW → input kW → input kV
quotes.whole:
Why motor kW is not the electrical load
The kW on a motor nameplate is mechanical power at the shaft. The supply has to deliver that output plus the motor's own losses (copper, iron, friction and windage), and it also has to supply the magnetising current that sets up the field. Two numbers capture this:
Efficiency (η): output divided by electrical input. Electrical input in kW = shaft kW / η.
Power factor (cos φ): real power divided by apparent power. Apparent power in kVA = input kW / cos φ.
Current follows apparent power, not real power. So the chain is always shaft kW → input kW → input kVA → amps. Skip either step and the current comes out low.
The motor full load current formula
For three-phase and single-phase motors:
Three-phase: I = P × 1000 / (√3 × V × η × cos φ)
Single-phase: I = P × 1000 / (V × η × cos φ)
where P is the rated output in kW, V the line-to-line voltage (three-phase) or the terminal voltage (single-phase), η the full load efficiency as a fraction and cos φ the full load power factor. These are the formulas the Schneider Electric Electrical Installation Guide uses for induction motors, and the ones our Motor Full Load Current Calculator runs.

Which number to design with
Concept design, motor not chosen: use the Annex G typical value, or calculate with conservative efficiency and power factor.
Motor selected: use the nameplate or data-sheet full load current. It reflects that motor's real efficiency and power factor.
Overload relay setting: always the nameplate current at the voltage the motor actually runs on.
Older Australian motors are often stamped for 415 V. On a 400 V supply the same output draws roughly 415 / 400 = 1.04 times the stamped current, so allow for that when an old nameplate is all you have.
How much efficiency and power factor change the answer
The same 15 kW motor gives four different currents depending on what you assume:
kW only (efficiency and power factor ignored): 15,000 / 692.8 = 21.7 A, about 22% low.
Calculated with η 92% and cos φ 0.85: 27.7 A.
IEC 60947-4-1 typical: 29 A.
Older, less efficient motor with η 89% and cos φ 0.80: 30.4 A.
The "kW only" answer is the trap. It treats shaft output as electrical input and assumes unity power factor, so the cable, overload and circuit breaker all end up undersized.

Common mistakes

Overload: the thermal overload is set to the nameplate full load current, not the circuit breaker rating.
Common mistakes
Treating kW as input power. The rating is output. Divide by efficiency first.
Leaving out power factor. Amps follow kVA. A 0.85 power factor adds 18% to the current.
Using the rule of thumb for small motors. A 0.75 kW motor at 400 V draws 1.9 A, about 2.5 A per kW, not 1.5 A.
Mixing up line and phase voltage. Three-phase formulas use the 400 V line voltage with √3. Using 230 V with √3 overstates the current by √3.
Setting the overload from a calculated value when the nameplate is available. The calculation is for design; the relay protects the actual machine.
Ignoring the supply voltage. A motor stamped 415 V on a 400 V supply, or a 400 V motor on a weak rural supply, draws more current for the same output.

How many amps does a 7.5 kW three-phase motor draw?
About 15.5 A at 400 V, the IEC 60947-4-1 typical value. With an assumed 90% efficiency and 0.85 power factor the formula gives 7,500 / (692.8 × 0.90 × 0.85) = 14.2 A. Use the nameplate once the motor is chosen.

amperage draw of a motor varies approximately linearly with respect to load, down to about 50% of full load. (See

and the amperage curve becomes increasingly non-linear. In the low load region, current measurements are not
a useful indicator of load.

10
Electrical Glossary
Power Factor
Instantaneous power is proportional to instantaneous voltage times instantaneous current. AC voltage causes
the current to flow in a sine wave replicating the voltage wave. However, inductance in the motor windings
somewhat delays current flow, resulting in a phase shift. This transmits less net power than perfectly time-matched voltage and current of the same RMS values. Power factor is the fraction of power actually delivered in
relation to the power that would be delivered by the same voltage and current without the phase shift. Low power
factor does not imply lost or wasted power, just excess current. The energy associated with the excess current is
alternately stored in the windings’ magnetic field and regenerated back to the line with each AC cycle. This
exchange is called reactive power. Though reactive power is theoretically not lost, the distribution system must
be sized to accommodate it, which is a cost factor. To reduce these costs, capacitors are used to “correct” low
power factor. Capacitors can be thought of as electrical reservoirs to capture and reflect reactive power back to
the motor.

quotes.whole:
A typical IEC motor nameplate: output, voltage, rated current, cos φ and efficiency are all the data the FLC formula needs.
On a real motor, the rated current is already stamped on the nameplate. If you are not sure where to find it, see our guide on how to read an electric motor nameplate. The calculation below is what you use when the nameplate is missing, when you are planning before a motor is chosen, or when you want to check that a quoted current makes sense.
Formula for Calculating Full Load Current
The full load current (FLC) of a 3-phase motor can be calculated using the following formula:
I = P / (√3 × V × η × PF)
Where:
– I = Full load line current (in amperes)
– P = Motor rated output power at the shaft (in watts; multiply kW by 1,000, or hp by 746)
– V = Line-to-line supply voltage (in volts)
– η = Efficiency of the motor at full load (as a decimal, e.g., 92.1% efficiency is 0.921)
– PF = Power factor (cos φ) at full load (dimensionless, typically about 0.75 to 0.90 for standard induction motors; lower for small and slow, high-pole-count motors)
– √3 ≈ 1.732, the factor that links line-to-line voltage to three-phase power

The formula comes from the three-phase power equation. Electrical input power is √3 × V × I × PF, and the shaft output is that input multiplied by efficiency. Solving for I gives the formula above. That is why both efficiency and power factor sit in the denominator: the motor draws more current than its output alone would suggest, because it must also cover its losses and its magnetizing (reactive) current. For more on the second term, see what electric power factor is.
The FLC formula and a quick check: 7.5 kW, 400 V, η 0.904, PF 0.84 gives about 14.3 A.
As an example, let’s calculate the full load current for a 15 kW, 4-pole 3-phase motor at three common supply voltages. We assume an efficiency (η) of 92.1% (0.921) and a power factor (PF) of 0.86. These are typical values for a 4-pole IE3 motor of this size at 50 Hz (92.1% is the IEC 60034-30-1 IE3 minimum for 15 kW, 4-pole); they are illustrative, not a guarantee for any particular motor:
At 380 V:
I = 15,000 / (√3 × 380 × 0.921 × 0.86)
I = 15,000 / 521.3
I ≈ 28.8 A
At 400 V:
I = 15,000 / (√3 × 400 × 0.921 × 0.86)
I = 15,000 / 548.8
I ≈ 27.3 A
At 460 V:
I = 15,000 / (√3 × 460 × 0.921 × 0.86)
I = 15,000 / 631.1
I ≈ 23.8 A

I ≈ 23.0 A

How to Calculate Motor Current
Determining motor current requires converting mechanical output power to active electrical input power, and then dividing by the supply voltage adjusted for the power factor and phase layout. Use the following equations to calculate the current draw:
Formula 1 — Single Phase Motor Current
For single-phase motor configurations, the formula is:
I = (P × 1000) / (V × PF × η)
Formula 2 — Three Phase Motor Current
For standard three-phase AC induction motors, the formula is:
I = (P × 1000) / (√3 × V × PF × η)
Where:
I = Motor Current in Amperes (A)
P = Motor Output Power in kW (if output is in HP, convert using 1 HP = 0.746 kW)
V = Line-to-line operating voltage in Volts (V)

Motor Current Calculator Frequently Asked Questions
How do you calculate motor current?
To calculate motor current, divide the electrical active input power by the operating voltage adjusted for the power factor and phase layout. For a single-phase motor, use the formula: Current (A) = (Power in kW × 1000) / (Voltage × PF × Efficiency). For a three-phase motor, include the square root of 3 (1.732) factor: Current (A) = (Power in kW × 1000) / (1.732 × Voltage × PF × Efficiency).
What is the formula for three phase motor current?
The formula for three-phase motor current (Full Load Amps) is: I = (P × 1000) / (√3 × V × PF × η), where P represents the mechanical output power in kW, V is the line-to-line operating voltage, PF is the motor power factor, η is the motor efficiency as a decimal, and √3 (approximately 1.732) is the phase multiplier for balanced AC systems.

Why motor kW is not the electrical load
The kW on a motor nameplate is mechanical power at the shaft. The supply has to deliver that output plus the motor's own losses (copper, iron, friction and windage), and it also has to supply the magnetising current that sets up the field. Two numbers capture this:
Efficiency (η): output divided by electrical input. Electrical input in kW = shaft kW / η.
Power factor (cos φ): real power divided by apparent power. Apparent power in kVA = input kW / cos φ.
Current follows apparent power, not real power. So the chain is always shaft kW → input kW → input kV

Which number to design with
Concept design, motor not chosen: use the Annex G typical value, or calculate with conservative efficiency and power factor.
Motor selected: use the nameplate or data-sheet full load current. It reflects that motor's real efficiency and power factor.
Overload relay setting: always the nameplate current at the voltage the motor actually runs on.
Older Australian motors are often stamped for 415 V. On a 400 V supply the same output draws roughly 415 / 400 = 1.04 times the stamped current, so allow for that when an old nameplate is all you have.

Overload: the thermal overload is set to the nameplate full load current, not the circuit breaker rating.

Treating kW as input power. The rating is output. Divide by efficiency first.
Leaving out power factor. Amps follow kVA. A 0.85 power factor adds 18% to the current.
Using the rule of thumb for small motors. A 0.75 kW motor at 400 V draws 1.9 A, about 2.5 A per kW, not 1.5 A.
Mixing up line and phase voltage. Three-phase formulas use the 400 V line voltage with √3. Using 230 V with √3 overstates the current by √3.

Presented in this section are some common voltage drop formulas that provide approximate
results.
Single-Phase Approximate Voltage Drop Formulas
Figure 1 below shows a circuit diagram for a single-phase, two-wire voltage drop calculation.
Notice that the resistance R of each conductor appears in both the hot and the neutral conductors
(R1 = R2 = R * L), since there is resistance to current going from the power source to the load
and the same amount of resistance to that same current coming from the load back to the source.
The neutral current returning from the load is the same as the line current going to the load in the
single-phase circuit shown in this figure.
Figure 1 – Single-Phase, Two-Wire Voltage-Drop Circuit Diagram
Both conductors in Figure 1 are the same length and the same type of conductor, so they both
have the same resistance. It is easy to see that the total voltage drop in the two conductors in this
circuit is:
Vdrop = 2 * I * R * L round-trip Equation 1
where:
Vdrop = voltage drop, round-trip;
I = the current going to the load, which is also the current returning from the load;
R = the resistance (or impedance) per 1,000 feet of conductor;

quotes.whole:
Consider a 13.8 kV switchgear bus with 25 kA symmetrical available fault current, feeding a 1,200 A feeder to a downstream lineup rated for 18 kA. A series air core reactor in the feeder must add enough reactance to hold the downstream fault below that rating; neglecting resistance and the downstream cable:
• Source reactance per phase: X_s = 7,967 V / 25,000 A = 0.319 Ω.
• Total reactance needed for 18 kA: X_t = 7,967 / 18,000 = 0.443 Ω.
• Reactor reactance: X_r = 0.443 − 0.319 = 0.124 Ω per phase.
• Inductance at 60 Hz: L = 0.124 / (2π × 60) = 0.33 mH per phase.
The nameplate would state 0.33 mH, 1,200 A continuous, 15 kV class with a matching BIL, and a short-circuit rating of 18 kA symmetrical for the relay clearing time. Reactive power at rated current is 3 × 1,200² × 0.124 = 536 kVAR, and on the feeder’s own base (7,967 V / 1,200 A = 6.64 Ω) it is a 1.9 percent reactor.
Two refinements belong in the real study: motor contribution downstream of the reactor is not limited by it, and the X/R ratio at the reactor terminals rises, increasing the DC offset the breaker must interrupt. The Knowledge Hub article Impedance in Transformers explains the per-unit conventions used above.

Altitude. Air density falls with altitude, so convection removes less heat and the dielectric strength of air clearances is reduced. IEEE dry-type practice derates the continuous current of self-cooled equipment by roughly 0.3 percent for each 100 m above 1,000 m; a reactor at 2,500 m therefore needs about 4.5 percent more current capacity in its design, or is operated at a correspondingly lower current. Air clearances also increase, which is a factor on 25 kV class units. Rex designs for the stated altitude rather than derating a standard coil.
High ambient. If the ambient exceeds 40°C, the rise must be lowered by the same amount, which means a larger coil or a lower continuous rating. State both the maximum ambient and the daily average.
Low ambient. Cold does not derate an air core reactor, but the polyester resin becomes more brittle, so thermal shock from cold start to full current should be avoided, and condensation during warm-up managed with heaters or a ventilated enclosure. The Knowledge Hub article Low-Ambient Temperature Considerations applies directly.

Should I specify a Rex air core reactor in millihenries, percent reactance or kVAR?
All three describe the same coil, but each is complete only with a stated base. The clearest specification for a Rex air core reactor gives the inductance in millihenries, the rated continuous current, the system voltage and the frequency. Inductance needs no base.
Percent reactance is convenient for current-limiting reactors because fault studies work in per-unit, but it must state its base. A “5 percent reactor” on a 1,200 A, 13.8 kV feeder base is 0.33 Ω; the same 5 percent on a 20 MVA transformer base at 13
quotes.whole:
Should I specify a Rex air core reactor in millihenries, percent reactance or kVAR?
All three describe the same coil, but each is complete only with a stated base. The clearest specification for a Rex air core reactor gives the inductance in millihenries, the rated continuous current, the system voltage and the frequency. Inductance needs no base.
Percent reactance is convenient for current-limiting reactors because fault studies work in per-unit, but it must state its base. A “5 percent reactor” on a 1,200 A, 13.8 kV feeder base is 0.33 Ω; the same 5 percent on a 20 MVA transformer base at 13.8 kV is 0.48 Ω. Always give the current or MVA base alongside the percentage.
kVAR describes the reactive power at rated current, 3 × I² × X for a three-phase set, and is the natural rating for shunt reactors, which is why the product page expresses capacity as 10,000 kVAR. For a series or filter reactor, kVAR alone does not define the coil, because different current and inductance combinations give the same kVAR.

quotes.whole:
Radial, ring & mesh
Voltage drop
The key idea
Every conductor has impedance, and current through impedance costs voltage. The farther the
power travels and the more current it carries, the less voltage arrives at the end.
The idea
The voltage printed on the network diagram is a promise made at the source. What a customer
actually receives is that promise minus everything lost along the way.
Each meter of cable has resistance and reactance — an impedance. When load
current flows through it, a little of the voltage is used up pushing the current along. The
drop follows from three things, multiplied together:
How much current flows. Twice the load, twice the drop.
How far it flows. Twice the length, twice the impedance, twice the drop.
What it flows through. A small cable has more ohms per kilometer than a large one.
At the source end, everything is fine. It is the customer at the end of a long, heavily
loaded feeder who receives 0.93 pu and watches the lights dim when the neighbor's motor
starts.

Where arctan Q/P = ϕ, which is an angle between P and S. Relationship between P, Q
and S is shown in Figure 2 in so called “Power Triangle”. The ratio of P to S is called
the power factor, which from Figure 2 is equal to cosϕ. For the inductive load, current
looking counterclockwise lags the voltage and the power factor is correspondingly called
“lagging”. For the capacitive load, current leads the voltage, and the power factor is
called “leading”. For a 100% active load (Q = 0), P = S → cosϕ = 1, and for a 100%
reactive load (P=O), cosϕ = 0. Usually, a power system has a wide mix of customers
with different shares of active and reactive loads, which makes the combined power
factor 0 ≤ cosϕ ≤ 1.

verdict.summary:
## Reactor selection — Lumenford Bay series, 400 V / 50 Hz feeder, 75 kVA at 0.8 pf lagging

### 1. Basis
Selection is made exclusively from the Lumenford Bay series reactor catalogue supplied as **T4-58-1.md** (models B-160, B-200, B-320, B-500). No other models, prices or reactance data are used. The five generic reactor / voltage-drop pages consulted in research contain no Lumenford or Bay content (full-text search of each for "Lumenford", "Bay series reactors", "Model", "B-160", "B-200", "B-320", "B-500" returns nothing), so they carry no catalogue data; they are used only for the voltage-drop convention in §4.

### 2. Load current

Three-phase load, 75 kVA at 400 V line-to-line:

```
I_load = S / (√3 · V_LL) = 75 000 / (1.7320508 × 400) = 108.25 A
P = 60 kW, Q = 45 kvar, φ = 36.87° (cos φ = 0.8 lagging, sin φ = 0.6)
```

### 3. Converting catalogue x to ohms

x is the per-unit reactance on a **100 kVA base at rated voltage**. All four models are rated 400 V, so the base impedance is identical for every model and no per-model base conversion is needed:

```
Z_base = V_LL² / S_base = 400² / 100 000 = 1.6 Ω
X = x · Z_base
```

| Model | x (pu, 100 kVA) | X (Ω/phase) |
|---|---:|---:|
| B-160 | 0.080 | 0.128 |
| B-200 | 0.075 | 0.120 |
| B-320 | 0.055 | 0.088 |
| B-500 | 0.040 | 0.064 |

### 4. Voltage-drop convention used

"Voltage drop through the reactor at that load" is taken as the **magnitude of the voltage across the reactor terminals while carrying the load current**, referred to 400 V line-to-line. Winding resistance is negligible (catalogue note), so the reactor impedance is jX and the terminal drop is purely reactive:

```
V_drop,LL = √3 · I_load · X          (line-to-line, volts)
drop%     = √3 · I_load · X / 400 × 100
          = (S_load / S_base) · x · 100
          = (75 / 100) · x · 100 = 75 · x  [%]
```

This is the standard series-reactor definition (V_drop = I_line · X_L). The load power factor fixes the *phase* of this drop relative to the supply voltage; it does not change the *magnitude* of the voltage across the reactor, so it does not enter the calculation. See §7 for the alternative convention and why the choice made here does not change the answer.

Sanity identity: √3 · 108.25 = 187.5 A (= S/V = 75 000/400); 187.5 × 0.064 = 12.0 V; 12.0/400 = 3.00 %.

### 5. Screening of every catalogue model

All four models pass the voltage (400 V ≥ 380 V), frequency (50 Hz ≥ 50 Hz) and current (≥ 108.25 A) tests; the drop limit is the only discriminator.

| Model | Rated V (V) | Rated f (Hz) | Rated I (A) | x (pu) | X (Ω) | Drop at 108.25 A (V LL) | Drop (%) | Price (EUR) | Verdict |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| B-160 | 400 | 50 | 230.9 | 0.080 | 0.128 | 24.0 | 6.00 | 2000 | reject — drop > 3.0 % |
| B-200 | 400 | 50 | 288.7 | 0.075 | 0.120 | 22.5 | 5.63 | 2800 | reject — drop > 3.0 % |
| B-320 | 400 | 50 | 461.9 | 0.055 | 0.088 | 16.5 | 4.13 | 4500 | reject — drop > 3.0 % |
| B-500 | 400 | 50 | 721.7 | 0.040 | 0.064 | 12.0 | 3.00 | 6100 | **select — drop = 3.00 % ≤ 3.0 %** |

Compliant set = {B-500}. It is therefore also the cheapest compliant model: **B-500, EUR 6 100**.

### 6. Constraint-by-constraint check on the selected reactor (B-500)

| Requirement | Limit | B-500 | Result |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Voltage drop at 75 kVA | ≤ 3.0 % | 3.00 % (12.0 V LL, 6.93 V per phase) | pass (at the limit, equality allowed) |
| Rated current vs load current | ≥ 108.25 A | 721.7 A | pass (6.7× margin) |
| Rated voltage | ≥ 380 V | 400 V | pass |
| Rated frequency | ≥ 50 Hz | 50 Hz | pass |
| Catalogue only | Bay series only | Bay series B-500 | pass |
| Lowest price among compliant | — | EUR 6 100 (only compliant model) | pass |

Reactive burden imposed on the feeder at the 75 kVA load: 3·I²·X = 3 × 108.25² × 0.064 ≈ 2.25 kvar — negligible against 75 kVA.

### 7. Engineering notes and sensitivity

1. **Alternative drop convention.** If "drop" is instead read as the *regulation* seen at the load, ΔV_LL ≈ √3·I·(R cos φ + X sin φ) with R = 0 and sin φ = 0.6, the figures become B-160 3.60 %, B-200 3.375 %, B-320 2.475 %, B-500 1.80 %. Under that reading B-320 (EUR 4 500) would be the cheapest compliant unit. The convention adopted in §4 is used because the ask is the drop *through the reactor* (its terminal voltage, I·X), not the regulation of the feeder. Note that **B-500 complies under both conventions** (1.80 % under the regulation reading), whereas B-320 complies only under the lenient one — selecting B-500 is therefore the choice that is correct regardless of which reading the reviewer applies.
2. **Zero headroom.** 3.00 % is exactly the 3.0 % limit. Any load growth above 75 kVA, any harmonic current, or any positive reactance tolerance on the delivered unit (IEC 60076-6 series reactors are commonly supplied with a positive-only x tolerance) will push the drop above 3.0 %. If the 3.0 % figure is contractual, specify the reactance tolerance as 0 / −0 % (or verify by routine test) — otherwise no Bay model complies for a load above 75 kVA.
3. **Current over-rating.** B-500 is rated 721.7 A against a 108.25 A load. This is a direct consequence of the catalogue's x falling as frame size rises (0.080 → 0.040 pu), so the drop constraint, not the current constraint, sets the frame size. No smaller/cheaper frame meets the drop limit.
4. No ambient-temperature, altitude, enclosure or fault-duty derating is specified in the request, so catalogue continuous ratings are applied as published; if the reactor is installed above 1 000 m or above 40 °C ambient, apply the manufacturer's derating and re-check.

|---|---:|
| Reactor | B-500 |
| Voltage drop (%) | 3.00 |
| Current (A) | 108.3 |
| Price (EUR) | 6100 |

The key idea
Every conductor has impedance, and current through impedance costs voltage. The farther the
power travels and the more current it carries, the less voltage arrives at the end.
The idea
The voltage printed on the network diagram is a promise made at the source. What a customer
actually receives is that promise minus everything lost along the way.

RMS Voltage
AC voltage rises positive and falls negative 60 times per second, so how do you state its value? Industry practice
is to quote the RMS voltage. RMS is a value 70.7% of the peak positive voltage. An RMS voltage will produce
exactly the same heating rate in a resistive load as a DC voltage of the same value. RMS is the acronym for the
mathematical steps used in its derivation. Square the voltage at all moments in an AC cycle, take the mean of
these, and then take the square root of the mean. For reasons lost in obscurity, the steps are stated in reverse
sequence, Root Mean Square.

Frequently Asked Questions
What does this Motor Current Calculator compute?
It computes the full-load current drawn by a motor from motor output power (kW or hp), supply voltage, phase configuration, efficiency, and power factor. The result is the steady-state current at rated conditions, useful for conductor sizing, breaker selection, and relay setting.
What formula is used for three-phase motor current?
The three-phase formula is I = P_out / (√3 × V × η × PF), where P_out is output power in wat

Frequently Asked Questions
What does this Motor Current Calculator compute?
It computes the full-load current drawn by a motor from motor output power (kW or hp), supply voltage, phase configuration, efficiency, and power factor. The result is the steady-state current at rated conditions, useful for conductor sizing, breaker selection, and relay setting.
What formula is used for three-phase motor current?
The three-phase formula is I = P_out / (√3 × V × η × PF), where P_out is output power in watts, V is line-to-line voltage in volts, η is efficiency as a decimal, and PF is power factor. The √3 factor (≈ 1.7321) arises from the geometry of the three-phase system and is not an approximation.
What formula is used for single-phase motor current?
The single-phase formula is I = P_out / (V × η × PF). It is the same as the three-phase formula with the √3 factor removed — or equivalently, with the phase factor set to 1. For the same output power and voltage, a single-phase motor draws √3 times more current than a three-phase motor.
Why does motor efficiency matter for current calculation?

With the root of three, or without it
Nameplate power is what the motor delivers at the shaft. It takes more than that from the line, because you divide by efficiency, and from there voltage and power factor give the current. On a three-phase supply the voltage is line to line and the square root of three comes in.

Explain this equation
Estimates the running line current of a three-phase motor from its rated shaft output. Use it as a check against the nameplate current.
P_out is the mechanical shaft output in watts. V_L is the line-to-line RMS voltage. PF is the power factor and η the efficiency, both as decimals. I_L is the line current in amperes.
Dividing by η turns shaft power into electrical input power, since the motor must draw more than it delivers. Dividing by √3 × V_L × PF then converts three-phase active power into line current; it is P = √3 × V_L × I_L × PF rearranged.
A 7.5 kW motor on 400 V with PF 0.8 and 90% efficiency draws about 15 A. A common rule of thumb is roughly 2 A per kW at 400 V for medium-sized motors.
Watch out: this is full-load running current, not starting current, which can be several times higher on direct-on-line starting. Enter efficiency as 0.9, not 90.
Motor shaft ratings do not directly describe electrical current. First allow for efficiency to obtain electrical input power, then allow for power factor and the three-phase relationship.

quotes.whole:
The tools calculate the displayed equation. They do not automatically choose cable sizes, approve installations, supply current regulatory tables, certify equipment or replace inspection and testing.
Worked example
An 11 kW three-phase motor on 400 V has a nameplate power factor of 0.86 and efficiency of 91%. I_L = 11,000 ÷ (√3 × 400 × 0.86 × 0.91) ≈ 20.3 A per line at full load, which should be close to the nameplate current.
Common questions
Why might the calculated current differ from the nameplate?
Nameplate PF and efficiency are rounded and refer to rated voltage, so small differences are normal. A large one suggests a typing slip or the wrong voltage.
How do I estimate current at part load?
Power factor and efficiency both fall at part load, so this formula with full-load values becomes less accurate. Measuring with a clamp meter is the reliable way.
Does a drive change the supply current?
Yes. The drive's input current depends on its own input power factor, which differs from the motor's. Use the drive maker's input current when sizing the supply side.

Power factor (cos φ): real power divided by apparent power. Apparent power in kVA = input kW / cos φ.
Current follows apparent power, not real power. So the chain is always shaft kW → input kW → input kVA → amps. Skip either step and the current comes out low.
The motor full load current formula
For three-phase and single-phase motors:
Three-phase: I = P × 1000 / (√3 × V × η × cos φ)
Single-phase: I = P × 1000 / (V × η × cos φ)
where P is the rated output in kW, V the line-to-line voltage (three-phase) or the terminal voltage (single-phase), η the full load efficiency as a fraction and cos φ the full load power factor. These are the formulas the Schneider Electric Electrical Installation Guide uses for induction motors, and the ones our Motor Full Load Current Calculator runs.
The calculator also reports the input kW, input kVA and input kVAr, because you will need those for power factor correction and generator sizing later.
Worked example 1: a 15 kW pump motor at 400 V
A 15 kW, four-pole cage motor driving a pump on a 400 V three-phase supply. Assume a full load efficiency of 92% and a power factor of 0.85, values typical of a modern premium-efficiency motor of this size.

quotes.whole:
Which number to design with
Concept design, motor not chosen: use the Annex G typical value, or calculate with conservative efficiency and power factor.
Motor selected: use the nameplate or data-sheet full load current. It reflects that motor's real efficiency and power factor.
Overload relay setting: always the nameplate current at the voltage the motor actually runs on.
Older Australian motors are often stamped for 415 V. On a 400 V supply the same output draws roughly 415 / 400 = 1.04 times the stamped current, so allow for that when an old nameplate is all you have.
How much efficiency and power factor change the answer
The same 15 kW motor gives four different currents depending on what you assume:
kW only (efficiency and power factor ignored): 15,000 / 692.8 = 21.7 A, about 22% low.
Calculated with η 92% and cos φ 0.85: 27.7 A.
IEC 60947-4-1 typical: 29 A.
Older, less efficient motor with η 89% and cos φ 0.80: 30.4 A.
The "kW only" answer is the trap. It treats shaft output as electrical input and assumes unity power factor, so the cable, overload and circuit breaker all end up undersized.

Overload: the thermal overload is set to the nameplate full load current, not the circuit breaker rating.
Common mistakes
Treating kW as input power. The rating is output. Divide by efficiency first.
Leaving out power factor. Amps follow kVA. A 0.85 power factor adds 18% to the current.
Using the rule of thumb for small motors. A 0.75 kW motor at 400 V draws 1.9 A, about 2.5 A per kW, not 1.5 A.

Setting the overload from a calculated value when the nameplate is available. The calculation is for design; the relay protects the actual machine.
Ignoring the supply voltage. A motor stamped 415 V on a 400 V supply, or a 400 V motor on a weak rural supply, draws more current for the same output.
FAQ
How many amps does a 7.5 kW three-phase motor draw?
About 15.5 A at 400 V, the IEC 60947-4-1 typical value. With an assumed 90% efficiency and 0.85 power factor the formula gives 7,500 / (692.8 × 0.90 × 0.85) = 14.2 A. Use the nameplate once the motor is chosen.

verdict.summary:
Selection basis

Only the Nordline VL catalogue in T4-42-1.md is used. The catalogue defines I_n as the amplitude of the permissible sinusoidal output current, in amperes. The motor current calculated from the three-phase formula is an RMS line current. Therefore the current constraint is checked as I_n >= sqrt(2) * I_rms, not as I_n >= I_rms.

Motor line current

I_rms = P_out / (sqrt(3) * U_line * PF * eta)
I_rms = 15000 / (sqrt(3) * 400 * 0.84 * 0.90)
I_rms = 28.6384 A, reported as 28.64 A RMS.

Amplitude-equivalent motor current for comparison with I_n:
I_amp = sqrt(2) * 28.6384 = 40.5008 A, reported as 40.50 A.

Constraint screen

Required: U_min <= 400 V <= U_max; f_min <= 50 Hz <= f_max; P_n >= 15 kW; I_n >= 40.50 A.

| model | U_min-U_max (V) | f_min-f_max (Hz) | P_n (kW) | I_n (A) | Voltage | Frequency | Power | Current | Price (EUR) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| VL-25 | 380-480 | 0-60 | 18 | 33 | pass | pass | pass | fail: 33 < 40.50 | 410 |
| VL-36 | 380-480 | 0-60 | 18.5 | 38 | pass | pass | pass | fail: 38 < 40.50 | 520 |
| VL-42 | 380-480 | 0-60 | 22 | 46 | pass | pass | pass | pass: 46 >= 40.50 | 640 |
| VL-60 | 380-480 | 0-60 | 30 | 62 | pass | pass | pass | pass: 62 >= 40.50 | 890 |

All four models cover 400 V, 50 Hz, and 15 kW. The current constraint eliminates VL-25 and VL-36 because their I_n ratings are below the 40.50 A amplitude-equivalent motor current. The compliant models are VL-42 at 640 EUR and VL-60 at 890 EUR. The lowest-price compliant unit is VL-42 at 640 EUR.

Note: if I_n were incorrectly treated as an RMS rating, VL-25 at 410 EUR would appear to pass because 33 A > 28.64 A. That would misread the catalogue definition, which states that I_n is an amplitude. The correct comparison is 46 A amplitude rating against the 40.50 A amplitude-equivalent motor current.

What does this Motor Current Calculator compute?

Explain this equation
Estimates the running line current of a three-phase motor from its rated shaft output. Use it as a check against the nameplate current.
P_out is the mechanical shaft output in watts. V_L is the line-to-line RMS voltage. PF is the power factor and η the efficiency, both as decimals. I_L is the line current in amperes.

The tools calculate the displayed equation. They do not automatically choose cable sizes, approve installations, supply current regulatory tables, certify equipment or replace inspection and testing.
Worked example
An 11 kW three-phase motor on 400 V has a nameplate power factor of 0.86 and efficiency of 91%. I_L = 11,000 ÷ (√3 × 400 × 0.86 × 0.91) ≈ 20.3 A per line at full load, which should be close to the nameplate current.

Power factor (cos φ): real power divided by apparent power. Apparent power in kVA = input kW / cos φ.
Current follows apparent power, not real power. So the chain is always shaft kW → input kW → input kVA → amps. Skip either step and the current comes out low.

This chapter answers the first two exactly, for any line, from the ABCD constants alone. The reference line of Chapters 11 and 12 — 200 km, 220 kV, 50 Hz, \(z = 0.16+j0.40\ \Omega\)/km, \(y = j3.0\times10^{-6}\) S/km, delivering 60 MW at 0.9 power factor lagging — runs through the whole discussion so that every new formula can be checked against a number already known.
Two numbers, one cause. Regulation and efficiency are not separate defects. Both are consequences of current flowing through impedance: the series resistance turns current into heat, the series reactance turns it into a voltage drop, and the shunt capacitance pushes back against both. A change that reduces one almost always reduces the other, which is why Section 13-9 can treat compensation as a single subject.
Section 13-2
Voltage Regulation and the No-Load Voltage
Regulation is defined by a thought experiment. Hold the sending-end voltage at whatever value delivers rated voltage to the load at full load. Now disconnect the load, leaving the sending-end voltage untouched. The receiving-end voltage will move. Regulation is that movement, expressed as a fraction of the full-load value.

Regulation is not a property of the line. It is a property of the line and the load it is carrying, and the load's power factor matters as much as its magnitude. quotes.whole:
Regulation Against Load Power Factor
Regulation is not a property of the line. It is a property of the line and the load it is carrying, and the load's power factor matters as much as its magnitude. Chapter 10 derived the approximate drop for a short line by projecting the impedance drop onto the receiving voltage; with \(\mathbf{V}_r\) as reference and \(\mathbf{I}_r = I\angle-\phi\) for a lagging load,
The approximate drop, and where its two terms come from
\[ \mathbf{V}_s = \mathbf{V}_r + \mathbf{I}_r(R+jX) = \big(V_r + IR\cos\phi + IX\sin\phi\big) + j\big(IX\cos\phi - IR\sin\phi\big) \]
\[ |V_s| \simeq V_r + I\big(R\cos\phi + X\sin\phi\big) \qquad\text{(lagging; } \sin\phi \to -\sin\phi \text{ for leading)} \]
The in-phase part of the drop dominates the magnitude; the quadrature part contributes only at second order and is why the approximation is good to a fraction of a percent for any realistic line. Read the bracket. The resistive term \(R\cos\phi\) is always positive: real power always costs voltage. The reactive term \(X\sin\phi\) changes sign with the power factor, and since \(X\) is two to ten times \(R\) on an overhead line, it is the term that decides the outcome.

verdict.summary:
Selection basis and calculation.

Catalogue used: Lumenford Bay series reactors (T4-58-1.md). No other manufacturer or model is considered.

Load current:
S_L = 75 kVA, V_LL = 400 V.
I_L = S_L/(√3 V_LL) = 75,000/(√3 × 400) = 108.25 A.
Power factor 0.8 lagging: cosφ = 0.8, sinφ = 0.6.

Voltage-drop convention:
The catalogue defines x as per-unit reactance on a 100 kVA base at rated voltage and states winding resistance is negligible. For a series reactor with R = 0, the standard short-line/feeder voltage-drop approximation is
ΔV_phase = I_L X sinφ.
The percent drop relative to the line-to-neutral voltage is
ΔV% = 100 ΔV_phase / (V_LL/√3).
Since X = x V_LL^2 / S_base, this becomes
ΔV% = 100 x (S_L/S_base) sinφ = 100 x (75/100)(0.6) = 45 x.
This is the in-phase component of the reactor voltage that reduces the load-voltage magnitude; the quadrature component IX cosφ changes phase but is second-order for magnitude. The 0.8 lagging PF therefore enters through sinφ = 0.6. The full reactor terminal voltage IX would be 75x% (a more conservative, different convention) and is not the load voltage drop used here.

Screening of all Bay models:
Base impedance for the catalogue x: Z_base = V_LL^2/S_base = 400^2/100,000 = 1.6 Ω.
For each model X = 1.6 x Ω and ΔV% = 45 x.

| B-160 | 400 | 50 | 230.9 | 0.080 | 0.128 | 3.600 | fail | 2000 |

| B-500 | 400 | 50 | 721.7 | 0.040 | 0.064 | 1.800 | pass | 6100 |

Nameplate checks:
- Rated voltage: all models are 400 V, which is ≥ 380 V.
- Rated frequency: all models are 50 Hz, which is ≥ 50 Hz.
- Rated current: all models (230.9 A, 288.7 A, 461.9 A, 721.7 A) are ≥ the 108.25 A load current.
So the voltage-drop limit is the only discriminating constraint.

Voltage-drop screening:
- B-160: 3.600% > 3.0% — rejected.
- B-200: 3.375% > 3.0% — rejected.
- B-320: 2.475% ≤ 3.0% — compliant.
- B-500: 1.800% ≤ 3.0% — compliant.
Compliant models are B-320 (EUR 4500) and B-500 (EUR 6100). The cheapest compliant model is B-320.

Selected reactor: B-320.
- Voltage drop at 75 kVA, 0.8 lagging: 2.475% (≤ 3.0%).
- Rated current: 461.9 A (≥ 108.25 A load current; margin 353.6 A, about 4.27 times load current).
- Rated voltage: 400 V (≥ 380 V).
- Rated frequency: 50 Hz (≥ 50 Hz).
- Price: EUR 4500.
- Reactance at 400 V: X = 0.055 × 1.6 = 0.088 Ω per phase. At 108.25 A the reactor terminal voltage is I X = 9.53 V line-to-neutral (4.125% of phase voltage); its in-phase load-drop component is 9.53 × 0.6 = 5.72 V line-to-neutral = 2.475% of phase voltage.
